paperInfo.subject: Divinity
paperInfo.paperName: Divinity A-Level Paper 1 — Prophets of the Old Testament

questions.questionText: Compare the phenomena of ecstatic prophecy (e.g., 1 Samuel 10 & 19) with classical eighth-century literary prophecy (Amos, Hosea, Isaiah). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Ecstatic Groups (Nebiim):** Band-based, music-induced frenzy, associated with royal shrines & military morale, little emphasis on social ethics [11 marks].
- **Classical Prophets:** Individual divine calls (*Amos 7, Isaiah 6*), direct "Thus says the Lord" moral indictment of injustice/idolatry, written oracle preservation [11 marks].
- **Continuity/Synthesis:** Traces of visionary ecstasy and symbolic acts persist in classical prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) [3 marks].

questions.questionText: Evaluate the role played by Samuel in Israel's transition from the period of the Judges to the Monarchy (1 Samuel 1–15). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Bridge Figure:** Last circuit judge & prophet-priest uniting tribal confederacy at Mizpah/Ramah [7 marks].
- **Ambiguity over Kingship:** Anti-monarchical warnings (1 Sam 8) vs pro-monarchical divine anointing of Saul and later David, insisting kings remain subordinate to covenant Torah [18 marks].

questions.questionText: Examine the religious and socio-political significance of Elijah's confrontation with Ahab and Jezebel on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18) and over Naboth's Vineyard (1 Kings 21). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Mount Carmel:** Combats Phoenician Baalism syncretism promoted by Jezebel—fire from heaven proves Yahweh sovereign over rain, fire, and Israel's exclusivity [13 marks].
- **Naboth's Vineyard:** Defends covenant tribal inheritance rights (*nahalah*) against royal tyranny—proving Israelite kings are subject to Yahweh's moral law, unlike absolutist Canaanite monarchs [12 marks].

questions.questionText: Discuss the significance of Elisha's miracles and his political involvement in Northern Israel and Aram (2 Kings 2–13). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Miracles:** Pastoral compassion for widows/sons of prophets (oil jar, Shunammite child, poisoned stew) and healing foreigner Naaman showing Yahweh's universal power [12 marks].
- **Politics:** Anoints Jehu to purge the House of Omri and counsels kings against Aramean raids ("King-maker" prophet) [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Explain Amos' teaching on Social Justice and Covenant Election (Amos 2:6–8; 3:1–2; 5:21–24), and assess why Amaziah rejected him at Bethel (Amos 7:10–17). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Social Justice:** Condemns selling the needy for silver/sandals, bribery at city gates, dishonest weights, luxurious "cows of Bashan", and hollow cultic sacrifices divorced from righteousness ("Let justice roll down like waters") [14 marks].
- **Bethel Confrontation:** Election brings heavier accountability ("You only have I known... therefore I will punish you"). Amaziah treats Amos as a subversive Judean professional prophet threatening state sanctuary [11 marks].

questions.questionText: "Amos is a prophet of unrelenting doom without any authentic message of hope." How far do you agree with reference to Amos 9:11–15? [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Evidence for Unrelenting Doom:** Five visions ending in "The end has come upon my people" (8:2), Bethel altar destruction, Day of the Lord as darkness not light (5:18) [13 marks].
- **Case for Authentic Hope:** Calls to "Seek the Lord and live" (5:4–6), "perhaps the Lord will be gracious to the remnant" (5:15), and scholarly debate on whether post-exilic Judean editors appended 9:11–15 ("Booth of David") [12 marks].

questions.questionText: Examine how Hosea's domestic experience with Gomer symbolises Israel's covenant infidelity, divine *hesed* (steadfast love), and ultimate restoration. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Domestic Symbolism (Ch 1–3):** Gomer's unfaithfulness & prophetic child names (Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, Lo-Ammi) dramatise Israel's political alliances and Baal fertility cult apostasy [12 marks].
- **Redemptive Hesed (Ch 2, 11, 14):** Hosea's costly repurchase of Gomer reveals Yahweh's agonising paternal love ("How can I give you up, O Ephraim?" 11:8) seeking knowledge of God (*da'at Elohim*) over empty sacrifice [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Analyse the significance of Isaiah's Temple Call Vision (Isaiah 6) for his understanding of God's holiness, Israel's obduracy, and the Remnant theology. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Holiness (*Qadosh*):** Seraphim hymn reveals God's moral majesty & Isaiah's cleansed lips (*"Woe is me"* → *"Here am I, send me"*) [10 marks].
- **Hardening & Remnant:** Paradoxical commission that dull hearts resist repentance until judgment leaves only a felled stump—yet "the holy seed is its stump" (*Shear-Jashub*: "A remnant shall return") [15 marks].

questions.questionText: Discuss the significance of Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy (Isaiah 7:10–17) in the historical context of the Syro-Ephraimite Crisis (734 BCE). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Historical Context:** Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Damascus threaten Jerusalem to force Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian coalition; Ahaz plans to appeal to Tiglath-Pileser III instead of trusting Yahweh [11 marks].
- **Sign of Immanuel:** "With us is God" serves both as urgent warning against faithless foreign alliances (Assyria will devastate Judah like a razor) and promise that David's line survives before the child knows good from evil [14 marks].

questions.questionText: Contrast Micah's condemnation of corrupt rulers, false prophets, and cultic ritualism with his vision of true religion in Micah 6:6–8. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Indictments:** Corrupt officials skinning the poor (3:2–3), land seizures (2:1–2), prophets who cry "Peace" when paid [12 marks].
- **Micah 6:8 Ethics:** Rejects extravagant burnt offerings ("thousands of rams / firstborn") in favour of covenant triad: **Do justice (*mishpat*), love mercy/steadfast love (*hesed*), and walk humbly (*tsana*) with your God** [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Evaluate the reasons why Jeremiah's Temple Sermon (Jeremiah 7 & 26) provoked near-fatal hostility from Jerusalem's religious and political establishment. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Challenge to Zion Inviolability Dogma:** Popular belief since 701 BCE held that Solomon's Temple guaranteed unconditional immunity ("The temple of the Lord!") [11 marks].
- **Conditional Covenant & Shiloh Precedent:** Jeremiah calls the Temple a "den of robbers" harbouring oppression and warns Yahweh will destroy Jerusalem like Shiloh unless Judah genuinely reforms society; contrast Baruch/princes defending him via Micah precedent [14 marks].

questions.questionText: Analyse Jeremiah's "Confessions" (Jeremiah 11–20) and explain what they reveal about the psychological cost of true prophetic vocation. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Content of Laments:** Isolation (forbidden marriage/mourning ch 16), persecution by family in Anathoth, stocks under Pashhur (20:1–6), crying "O Lord, you have deceived me" (20:7) [13 marks].
- **Theological Insight:** Prophetic authority rests not on human bravado or popularity, but on inescapable inner compulsion ("fire shut up in my bones") and raw honest dialogue with God [12 marks].

questions.questionText: Assess the revolutionary elements of Jeremiah's New Covenant prophecy (Jeremiah 31:31–34) compared with the Mosaic Sinai Covenant. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Failure of Old Covenant:** Written on stone tablets, repeatedly broken despite prophetic warnings, leading to 587 BCE exile [9 marks].
- **New Covenant Breakthrough:** Law written internally on the heart, unmediated personal knowledge of God across all ages ("No longer teach neighbour"), unconditional divine forgiveness of sins, yet retaining continuity with Yahweh's Torah [16 marks].

questions.questionText: Examine Ezekiel's teaching on Individual Moral Responsibility (Ezekiel 18) and the Watchman (Ezekiel 3 & 33) among the Babylonian exiles. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Refuting "Sour Grapes" Fatalism:** Exiles blamed ancestral sins for disaster; Ezekiel insists "the soul that sins shall die"—each generation and individual may repent and live righteously [13 marks].
- **Watchman Accountability:** Prophet is personally liable before God to warn sinners clearly; once warned, responsibility shifts entirely to the listener [12 marks].

questions.questionText: Explain the vision of the Valley of Dry Bones (Ezekiel 37:1–14) and evaluate its theological message of national resurrection and universal divine sovereignty. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Exilic Despair:** "Our bones are dried up, our hope is lost" after Jerusalem's fall [7 marks].
- **Theology of Restoration:** Prophetic word + divine Spirit (*Ruach*) breathe physical and spiritual life into dead Israel—not by Israel's merit ("Not for your sake" 36:22) but to vindicate Yahweh's holy name among the nations [18 marks].

questions.questionText: Evaluate the identity and theological mission of the "Suffering Servant" in Deutero-Isaiah (Isaiah 42, 49, 50, 52:13–53:12). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Four Servant Songs:** Gentle mission establishing justice (42), light to the Gentiles (49), obedient endurance (50), vicarious atonement wounded for others' transgressions (53) [13 marks].
- **Identity Debate:** Collective faithful Israel/remnant, an ideal future Davidic messiah, the anonymous exilic prophet himself, or Christological NT fulfilment [12 marks].

questions.questionText: Discuss how prophets used Symbolic Actions (e.g., Isaiah going barefoot, Jeremiah's linen loincloth/wooden yoke, Ezekiel's siege brick) to communicate urgent divine messages. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Purpose:** Not mere visual theatre; in Hebrew thought (*dabar* = word-deed), prophetic acts set God's judgment or deliverance irrevocably in motion [10 marks].
- **Examples & Analysis:** Isaiah 20 (captivity to Assyria), Jeremiah 13 (spoilt pride), Jeremiah 27–28 (Nebuchadnezzar yoke vs Hananiah), Ezekiel 4–5 (siege starvation & shaved hair) [15 marks].

questions.questionText: Analyse the criteria by which true prophets could be distinguished from false prophets in Old Testament Israel (Deuteronomy 13, 18; 1 Kings 22; Jeremiah 23 & 28). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Biblical Tests:** Fulfilment of prediction (Deut 18:22), loyalty to Yahweh's exclusive worship (Deut 13), moral courage to rebuke sin rather than flatter rulers with "Peace, peace" (Micah 3, Jer 23), personal sacrifice [15 marks].
- **Dilemma of Immediacy (Micaiah vs Zedekiah; Jeremiah vs Hananiah):** When prophets invoke Yahweh in conflicting ways, immediate proof is hard—requiring moral/theological discernment [10 marks].

questions.questionText: Assess the importance of "False Religion and Empty Ritualism" across Amos, Isaiah 1, and Jeremiah 7, asking whether the prophets rejected sacrificial worship altogether. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Prophetic Attack:** Amos 5:21 ("I hate, I despise your feasts"), Isaiah 1:11–17 ("stop bringing meaningless offerings... defend the orphan & widow") [12 marks].
- **Evaluation:** Prophets did NOT abolish cultic worship itself; rather, they rejected magical reliance on sacrifice without ethical obedience, compassion, and social righteousness (*hesed* and *mishpat*) [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Examine how Deutero-Isaiah (Isaiah 40–55) develops radical Monotheism, Creation theology, and Universal Salvation for Babylonian exiles. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Radical Monotheism:** Yahweh is Creator of earth's ends ("Beside Me there is no god" 45:5); Babylonian idols are lifeless carved wood mocked by satire (44:9–20) [12 marks].
- **Universalism & Cyrus:** Yahweh sovereignly commissions Persian King Cyrus as His "anointed" deliverer and summons Israel to shine as "a light to the nations" (49:6) [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Compare the call experiences of Moses (Exodus 3), Isaiah (Isaiah 6), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1), and Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1–3). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Common Literary Structure (Call Form):** Divine encounter/theophany, commissioning, human objection/inadequacy ("slow of speech", "unclean lips", "only a youth"), divine reassurance & enabling sign [15 marks].
- **Distinctive Emphases:** Isaiah volunteers amid Temple holiness; Jeremiah feels pre-natal compulsion yet timid vulnerability; Ezekiel experiences mobile transcendence of God's glory (*kabod*) in pagan Babylon [10 marks].

questions.questionText: Evaluate Nathan's rebuke of King David (2 Samuel 12) and compare Nathan's prophetic courage with Elijah or Amos. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Nathan's Parable (Rich Man & Poor Man's Ewe Lamb):** Cleverly bypasses royal defensiveness so David condemns himself before hearing *"You are the man!"* [12 marks].
- **Comparison:** Like Elijah rebuking Ahab over Naboth and Amos confronting Bethel priest Amaziah, Nathan demonstrates royal accountability to Torah justice—crucial precedent for civic truth-telling today [13 marks].

questions.questionText: Discuss the theme of "The Day of the Lord" (*Yom Yahweh*) from Amos to Zephaniah and Joel, showing how classical prophets inverted popular optimism. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Popular Expectation:** Israel expected miraculous military victory, light, and material prosperity over Gentile foes [8 marks].
- **Prophetic Reversal:** Amos 5:18 warns it is "darkness and not light" purging Israel's own injustice; Zephaniah broadens it to cosmic judgment sparing only the humble remnant; Joel pairs locust judgment with Spirit outpouring (Joel 2:28) [17 marks].

questions.questionText: Examine the post-exilic encouragement of Haggai and Zechariah (1–8) in rebuilding the Second Temple (520–516 BCE). [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Context of Apathy:** Returned exiles prioritised panelled private houses over ruined Temple amid crop failure (Hag 1:4–9) [9 marks].
- **Haggai & Zechariah:** Link covenant fidelity to Temple reconstruction, promising "Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit" (Zech 4:6) alongside joint leadership of Joshua (high priest) and Zerubbabel (Davidic governor) [16 marks].

questions.questionText: Evaluate the relevance of eighth-century Old Testament prophetic teaching on corruption, wealth disparity, and land rights to contemporary Zimbabwean society. [25 marks]
questions.explanation:
### Mark Scheme [25 marks]
- **Textual Grounding:** Amos 5/8 (bribery in courts, exploiting workers, rigging scales), Isaiah 5:8 ("joining house to house & field to field"), Micah 2–3, 1 Kings 21 [12 marks].
- **Contemporary Application:** Critique of public corruption, wage injustice, environmental/land stewardship, and empty outward religiosity without ethical integrity—grounded balanced against secular economic nuance [13 marks].
